newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks edge up after robust gains fade.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks edge up after robust gains fade.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks eked out a small gain Tuesday, extending their recovery from Friday's sell-off, but the session's strong upward momentum was tempered by a late retreat in technology shares.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 9.31 points at 6,473.25 after racking up a mid-afternoon gain of nearly 50 points. On Monday, it surged 82 points.
The technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index was off 3.72 to 1,312.55, one day after closing at a new high.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,378 to 1,123 on active volume of 446 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts said investors' grew more confident for the second straight day after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's cautionary comments about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets sent stocks into a tailspin Friday.

The Fed chief's words, which were interpreted to mean that the central bank might step in to cool things off by raising interest rates, sparked a sell-off Friday of 145 points in the Dow before it rallied to end with a loss of 55 points.

"It's like Greenspan never said what he said. The spin on that is: It's one thing to use rhetoric and another to use policy," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "He's not going to bring the economy down by trying to stop IBM from going higher. It was a shot across the bow."
Earlier in the session, investors snapped up blue-chip stocks and semiconductor-related issues on an upbeat book-to-bill report, which is a gauge of the semiconductor industry's activity.

The November book-to-bill ratio rose to 1.15 from 1.11 in October, vs. expectations for a flat to slightly higher reading. The ratio means that manufacturers received $115 in new orders last month for every $100 in shipments.
But the jump in technology stocks later wafted away on profit-taking.
Semiconductorchip giant Intel lost one to 129-1/8, Micron fell 1-1/8 to 34 and Cypress Semiconductor was off 1/8 to 15-3/8.

"The tech sector is going to be volatile to the nth degree over the next several weeks," said Charlie Crane, director of research at Spears Benzak Salomon & Farrell. "Many stocks have been riding the coat tails on stocks like IBM and Intel, some with less justification than others. Many will deliver satisfactory earnings."

Among special situations, Black & Decker slumped 6-1/4 to 31-3/8 after forecasting its fourth-quarter and 1996 results would fall below expectations. It also warned that its 1997 first-quarter earnings will fall below year-ago levels.
Philip Morris rose 2-5/8 to 116-7/8 after Goldman Sachs on Monday raised its 12-month price target for the stock to $135 from $125.
Komag Inc., a maker of thin-film media for computer hard disk drives, slumped 5-7/8 to 27-1/4 after warning that its fourth-quarter results will be disappointing.
Stone Energy surged 2-1/4 to 25-7/8 on news that it expects to test "a significant discovery well" drilled in a natural gas field in federal waters offshore Louisiana.
EXCEL Communications lost 4-3/4 to 23-1/4. The company forecast its fourth-quarter results will fall below analysts' projections.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 2.22 to 747.54. The American Stock Exchange index was up 0.31 to 590.79.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.79 to 393.90. The average share was down 8 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,250.317 down 13.475 or 0.19 percent.
